name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
title: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
answer: The threshold of machine authorship asks when a work produced with generative AI counts as authored by a person, and when it does not. It sits inside emerging legal frameworks, where copyright offices, courts and legislatures are drawing lines between human creation and machine output. The question reaches text, images, music and code, and it decides who, if anyone, can hold rights in the result. It is a threshold question because everything downstream, ownership, licensing, infringement, depends on the answer.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: The threshold of machine authorship asks when a work produced with generative AI counts as authored by a person, and when it does not. It sits inside emerging legal frameworks, where copyright offices, courts and legislatures are drawing lines between human creation and machine output. The question reaches text, images, music and code, and it decides who, if anyone, can hold rights in the result. It is a threshold question because everything downstream, ownership, licensing, infringement, depends on the answer.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the ordinary machinery of copyright and contract: registration systems, licensing terms, platform policies and the records that show how a work was made. Practitioners rely on prompt logs, model versions, training data disclosures and edit histories to reconstruct the human contribution. This site tracks 150 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, alongside 29 AI case law precedents, which together form the working record of how these thresholds are being tested. Compliance teams map those materials against 229 regulation pages and 7166 state AI bills.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysis usually starts by separating the human contribution from the machine contribution, then asking whether the human part is expressive and fixed. Reviewers compare drafts, prompts, selections and arrangements, because the law tends to reward the choices a person actually made. Registration practice, office guidance and litigation outcomes are read together, since a rule announced in one forum often surfaces in another. The method is documentary: build a defensible record of authorship before the question is disputed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on disclosure, provenance and the terms attached to the tools used. A work with thin human authorship may fail registration, may not support an infringement claim, and may carry warranties the creator cannot meet. Provenance matters for both defence and enforcement, so versioning, model identity and source records are treated as evidence rather than housekeeping. The 688 glossary terms on this site exist partly because the vocabulary of authorship, originality and fixation is contested and shifting.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the threshold to move through case law and registration practice rather than a single statute, with offices and courts filling gaps as they arise. More disputes will test how much selection, arrangement or revision is enough, and licensing markets will price the uncertainty. Tools and platforms will keep changing faster than the rules, so records and disclosure habits will matter more, not less. The 850 AI tools tracked here suggest the volume of output will keep the question live for years.
